title: Budgeting & Saving Money
objectives: Set financial goals and save money
target_phrases: How much do I earn per month?
I need to save money for...
This is a need / This is a want

dialogue.title: Learning to Budget
dialogue.context: Ahmed talks to his friend Lisa about creating a budget and saving money. Lisa is good with money and helps him.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Hi Ahmed! How's the new job going?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: It's going well, but I'm worried about money. I don't know where all my money goes each month.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Sounds like you need a budget! It's not hard. First, how much do you earn per month after taxes?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: About $2,400 per month. Is that enough?

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: That depends on your expenses. Let's write them down. What's your rent?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Rent is $900. Then I have utilities, phone, food, and gas for my car.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Okay, those are all needs - things you must pay for. Do you have any wants - things you don't really need but enjoy?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I eat out a lot - maybe $300 per month. And I have a gym membership for $50.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: That's where you can save! Eating out is expensive. If you cook more at home, you could save $200 a month. That's $2,400 a year!

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Wow, I never thought about it that way. What should I do with the money I save?

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.text: Put it in your savings account. Try to save at least $200 per month. That's your emergency fund for unexpected expenses.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Great advice! I'm going to start tracking my spending and cut down on eating out. Thank you, Lisa!

examples: I earn $2,400 per month after taxes
I make $18 per hour at my job
My paycheck is $1,200 every two weeks
I bring home about $2,000 per month
My monthly income is $2,500

pattern_drills.pattern: [Item] is a need / [Item] is a want
examples: Rent is a need - I must have a place to live
A new TV is a want - I don't really need it
Food is a need - everyone must eat
Going to movies is a want - it's entertainment
Electricity is a need - I use it every day

pattern_drills.pattern: I'm trying to save money for [goal]
examples: I'm trying to save money for a car
I'm trying to save money for emergencies
I'm trying to save money for my education
I'm trying to save money for my family
I'm trying to save money for a vacation

listening_exercises.transcript: The 50-30-20 rule is a simple way to budget. Spend 50% of your income on needs like rent, food, and bills. Spend 30% on wants like entertainment and hobbies. Save 20% for emergencies and future goals. For example, if you earn $2,000 per month, spend $1,000 on needs, $600 on wants, and save $400.
listening_exercises.question: According to the 50-30-20 rule, how much should you save if you earn $2,000?

listening_exercises.transcript: An emergency fund is money saved for unexpected expenses - like if your car breaks down or you lose your job. Financial experts recommend saving 3 to 6 months of expenses. If your monthly expenses are $1,500, you should save $4,500 to $9,000. It sounds like a lot, but start small. Even $500 can help in an emergency.
listening_exercises.question: What is an emergency fund for?

listening_exercises.transcript: Here are five ways to cut costs: First, cook at home instead of eating out - you can save $200 or more per month. Second, cancel subscriptions you don't use. Third, use public transportation instead of driving when possible. Fourth, buy generic brands instead of name brands. Fifth, make coffee at home instead of buying it. Small changes add up to big savings!
listening_exercises.question: How much can you save by cooking at home?

speaking_tasks.prompt: Explain your monthly budget. Record yourself saying: 'I earn [amount] per month. My biggest expenses are rent, food, and [other]. I try to save [amount] each month.' Talk for at least 30 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: I earn $2,400 per month from my job. My biggest expenses are rent, which is $900, and food, which is about $400. I also pay for my phone, utilities, and gas. That's about $1,500 total for needs. I spend $300 on wants like entertainment. I try to save $400 each month for emergencies and future goals.

speaking_tasks.prompt: Give advice to a friend who spends too much money. Record yourself giving 3 tips for saving money. Speak for at least 25 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Here's my advice for saving money. First, track all your spending for one month. You'll be surprised where your money goes. Second, cook at home more often. Eating out is very expensive. Third, set up automatic transfers to your savings account. If you save before you spend, you won't miss the money. These tips really work!

writing_tasks.prompt: Create a simple budget. Write your monthly income and list 5 expenses (rent, food, phone, etc.). Then write how much you want to save. Use numbers.
writing_tasks.example: My Monthly Budget: I earn $2,400 per month. My expenses are: rent $900, food $400, phone $60, utilities $100, and gas $150. That's $1,610 for needs. I spend $300 on wants like eating out and entertainment. My total expenses are $1,910. I save $400 per month. This leaves me $90 extra for emergencies. I'm trying to increase my savings to $500 per month.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write about the difference between needs and wants. Give 3 examples of needs and 3 examples of wants. Explain why the difference matters.
writing_tasks.example: Needs and wants are different. Needs are things you must have to live. Examples of needs are: rent or housing, food, and utilities like water and electricity. Wants are things you enjoy but don't really need. Examples of wants are: cable TV, eating at restaurants, and new clothes when your old clothes are fine. Understanding the difference helps you save money. When you're on a tight budget, pay for needs first, then wants if you have money left over.

grammar_focus.title: Too much / Too many
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'too much' with uncountable nouns. Use 'too many' with countable nouns. Both mean 'more than is good or necessary'.
examples: I spend too much money on food. (money = uncountable)
I have too many expenses. (expenses = countable)
She spends too much time shopping. (time = uncountable)
They buy too many things they don't need. (things = countable)

practice.sentence: I spend ___ much money on eating out.
He has ___ many bills to pay.

grammar_focus.title: Comparative and Superlative
grammar_focus.explanation: Use comparatives to compare two things. Use superlatives for three or more.
examples: Cooking at home is cheaper than eating out. (comparative)
Public transportation is cheaper than driving. (comparative)
This is my biggest expense. (superlative)
Saving money is the most important goal. (superlative)

practice.sentence: This is the ___ way to save.

grammar_focus.title: Expressing Goals with 'trying to' and 'want to'
grammar_focus.explanation: Use 'I'm trying to' for goals you're working on. Use 'I want to' for goals you hope to achieve.
examples: I'm trying to save $500 per month. (currently working on it)
I want to buy a car next year. (future goal)
She's trying to spend less on clothes. (current effort)
They want to save for a house. (future goal)

practice.sentence: I ___ to buy a car next year.

cultural_notes: Americans save an average of only 3-5% of their income - financial experts recommend 20%.
The 50-30-20 rule is a popular budgeting method: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings.
Many Americans live 'paycheck to paycheck' with no emergency savings.
Apps like Mint, YNAB (You Need A Budget), and EveryDollar can help you track spending.
Credit card debt is common but dangerous - the interest rates are very high (15-25%).
Many employers offer 401(k) retirement plans and will match your contributions - free money!
Community colleges offer free financial literacy classes to help people learn about money.
